newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gives Chile positive sign on planes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives Chile positive sign on planes.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has given Chile a positive sign that the United States would look favorably on the sale of U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets to that country, officials said on Wednesday.

During talks with Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza, Albright "explained the rationale for our new arms policy and the fact that we would be prepared to consider that sale," one senior U.S. official told Reuters.
Albright did not say definitely that Washington would approve the sale, he said.
But her discussion with the minister made clear that the adminstration would consider the deal in a positive light, the official said.
Lockheed and McDonnell Douglas are competing the two U.S. firms involved.

President Bill Clinton made the sale possible when, in a major boost for Latin America and American arms dealers, he ended on Aug. 1 a 20-year-old ban on the sale of high-tech weaponry to Latin America.

Analysts say resumed sales from U.S. makers desperate for new markets since the end of the Cold War were inevitable after Peru went shopping in Eastern Europe and Chile started looking at European planes if it could not buy the U.S. F-16s it really wanted.
U.S. critics of Clinton's decision to lift the ban fear it will trigger an arms race in the region and undermine attempts by Latin American countries to strengthen their incipient democracies.
But regional officials say while the decision is likely to increase military spending in the region, it should not trigger an arms race.
Albright stressed on Wednesday at a joint news conference with Insulza that under the new policy each country's request would be decided on a case-by-case basis.
She did not make a public pitch for the U.S. firms. "It is obviously up to Chile to decide what it wishes to do in modernizing its air force," was all she said.
Insulza objected that the media spotlight was on Chile when the new arms sales policy affected the region, not just one country.
Albright stressed the importance of concluding a comprehensive trade agreement with Chile and hailed bilateral ties between Washington and Santiago.

She said she would discuss with Insulza many issues including Clinton's request for special authority "for the purpose of securing a comprehensive trade agreement with Chile and of moving ahead on our overall global trade agenda."

Clinton last week said obtaining from Congress fast-track approval of trade agreements -- meaning Congress gives up its right to amend the deal in favor of a straight yes or no vote -- was one of his priorities for 1997.

The administration wants the authority immediately to negotiate a trade agreement with Chile, which already has separate pacts with Canada and Mexico -- the U.S. partners in the North American Free Trade Agreeemnt.

But it hopes to expand NAFTA into a free trade pact covering all of North and South America, pursue separate trade negotiations with Asian-Pacific nations and conduct further global negotiations under the World Trade Organization.

U.S. officials have acknowledged, however, that Clinton faces a major challenge in obtaining this authority because many congressmen question the need for additional trade pacts, despite the importance of exports to the U.S. economy.

On Aug. 6, Richard Brown, U.S. senior coordinator of the Summit of the Americas, said in Buenos Aires the United States was leaning toward a bilateral trade pact with Chile rather than its full entry into NAFTA in part because Chile has negotiated separate free trade pacts with Mexico and Canada.

Clinton is to visit Chile for the second Summit of the Americas scheduled for April 1998 in Santiago. The summit is expected to launch negotiations to form the Americas Free Trade Agreement -- a hemisphere-wide pact --by the year 2005.
